name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade
blurb: In a classroom in Finland, seventh graders were given an unusual writing partner. A program called the Poetry Machine offered each student a draft poem, and the students were free to change it however they liked.
title: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade
answer: In a classroom in Finland, seventh graders were given an unusual writing partner. A program called the Poetry Machine offered each student a draft poem, and the students were free to change it however they liked.

papers.why: Useful as a catalog of writing tool types students already use, and as a caution: the sample is four teachers and the outcome is perception, not measured writing.
papers.title: The impact of AI writing tools on the content and organization of students’ writing: EFL teachers’ perspective
papers.caveat: Four teachers, higher education, perceptions only. Weak evidence despite 484 citations.
papers.finding: Interviews with four EFL teachers at three Indonesian universities about AI writing tools (Quillbot, WordTune, Jenni, ChatGPT, Paperpal, Copy.ai, Essay Writer). All reported improved content and organization in student writing.

papers.why: The only randomized evidence in the set, and it supports the book's feedback before grades pattern: AI feedback on drafts is worth doing, cheap, and motivating, while learning transfer needs repeated cycles, not one session. The prompt design is a ready made template for Chapter 17.
papers.title: Using LLMs to bring evidence-based feedback into the classroom: AI-generated feedback increases secondary students’ text revision, motivation, and positive emotions
papers.caveat: One session, one task, grade 10, foreign language writing, no comparison to teacher feedback, and students were not told the feedback came from AI. Feedback quality was not checked per student. Novelty effects cannot be ruled out. Effects on a new task were not significant.
papers.finding: Randomized controlled study, 459 Grade 10 students in German academic track schools, May to June 2023, one 90 minute lesson. Students wrote a TOEFL style argumentative essay in English, then half received GPT-3.5-turbo feedback and half only an instruction to revise. Feedback raised revision quality (d = 0.19), motivation for future writing tasks (d = 0.36), positive emotions (d = 0.34), and perceived usefulness (d = 1.19). It did not raise performance on a new essay written the same day. The prompt followed Hattie and Timperley: hints and examples on structure, content, and language, in a table, quoting the student text, with the model told the writers were upper secondary foreign language learners, temperature 0. Perceived usefulness averaged only 3.7 of 7, so quality has room to improve.

papers.why: The most complete taxonomy of writing tools in the set, with a workable division of labor for Chapter 6 (AI for sentence level, teacher for argument and structure) and a ready made case for Chapter 13 on machine translation as a learning tool for English learners rather than a banned shortcut.
papers.title: AI in the Foreign Language Classroom: A Pedagogical Overview of Automated Writing Assistance Tools
papers.caveat: Higher education and second language focus, pre ChatGPT (ended 2022 with GPT-3). Single author review. Many underlying studies are short term and industry affiliated.
papers.finding: PRISMA review of 104 Scopus papers (2017 to 2022) on AI writing assistance in tertiary language classrooms. Four tool types: automated writing evaluation (Criterion, MY Access, WriteToLearn), automated corrective feedback editors (Grammarly, ProWritingAid, Ginger), machine translation (Google Translate), and GPT text generators. Evidence is mixed and often vendor affiliated, with few control groups. AWE helps most when used early in drafting, improves lexical and grammar accuracy more than content or structure, and rarely shows long term learning. Grammarly over and under flags errors and is best used alongside teacher feedback, not alone. Students mostly use machine translation to look up words and phrases, not to translate whole texts, and teacher mediated training on post editing produces gains. Consensus across the reviewed studies: ban and boycott approaches fail; use a hybrid where AI handles sentence level issues and the teacher handles higher order ones, with peer review in between; build calibrated trust by teaching students what the tools can and cannot do; and treat implementation ecologically because results vary wildly by context.

papers.why: A balanced list of benefits and harms in teachers' words for the Chapter 6 integrity section.
papers.title: Is ChatGPT an evil or an angel for second language education and research? A phenomenographic study of research‐active EFL teachers’ perceptions
papers.caveat: Abstract only, closed access. Iranian higher education context.
papers.finding: Phenomenographic interviews with 30 Iranian EFL teachers. Potentials: learner autonomy, personalized learning, lower teacher workload, rubric design, summarizing papers. Pitfalls: loss of creativity and integrity, cheating on online exams, misinformation, high tech plagiarism. Offers practical suggestions for educators.

papers.why: Source labels bias students' judgment of feedback.
papers.title: Can students judge like experts? A large-scale study on the pedagogical quality of AI and human personalized formative feedback
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: 979 feedback pieces: AI and human formative feedback had comparable pedagogical quality; both weak on metacognition. 472 STEM students judged feedback by who they believed wrote it, not its actual quality.

papers.why: Gives a concrete classroom routine for AI feedback.
papers.title: Stop perfecting the feedback, start supporting the uptake: rethinking AI in writing instruction
papers.finding: Argues AI feedback uptake is low in K-12 and proposes a five-phase model: draft, AI feedback, individual revision, peer discussion, whole-class reflection with teacher as facilitator.

papers.why: Feedback type design matters.
papers.title: Directive, metacognitive, or a blend of both? A comparison of AI-generated feedback types on student engagement, confidence, and outcomes
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Compared directive, metacognitive, and blended AI feedback on engagement, confidence, and outcomes.

papers.why: AI feedback's value is redistributing teacher effort, not beating teachers.
papers.title: Comparing Teacher and AI-Generated Feedback in the Writing Classroom: Experimental Results from Secondary School Classrooms
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale
papers.caveat: Two sessions, feedback given once; immediate condition confounded with same-session second task; prompt did not include praise; sample may be underpowered per authors.
papers.finding: Within-class randomized trial, German grades 10-11 EFL writing (N=391): teacher-written feedback vs delayed GPT-4 feedback vs immediate GPT-4 feedback. No significant differences in revision performance, second-task performance, or revision time. Bayesian analysis: teacher feedback likely slightly better for transfer to a second task and for how positive feedback felt. Immediate AI feedback was rated more useful and more motivating. Immediacy alone did not improve performance.

papers.why: Feedback that is not used does nothing; uptake must be designed into lessons.
papers.title: Feedback from Generative AI: Correlates of Student Engagement in Text Revision from 655 Classes from Primary and Secondary School
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
papers.caveat: Vendor trial data, no student demographics or prompt; engagement is a one-character proxy; novelty of a new tool may cut either way.
papers.finding: Commercial GenAI (GPT-4) feedback platform, Germany, Nov 2023: 655 teacher-designed tasks, 14,236 students, grades 1-12. 48% (6,889) did not change a single character after feedback. Rates were flat across grade bands (primary 48% engaged, grades 5-6 49%, 7-9 51%, 10-11 52%, upper secondary 51%), task types (47-51%), and languages. No linguistic feature of drafts or feedback predicted engagement. Only 20 of 655 classes had every student revise; 27 had none.

papers.why: Feedback works best when turned into a few personal revision goals.
papers.title: Individualizing goal-setting interventions using automated writing evaluation to support secondary school students’ text revisions
papers.finding: 345 German upper secondary ESL students: individualized goal-setting based on automated writing evaluation scores produced the largest revision gains.

papers.why: Teachers remain better; AI fits early drafts.
papers.title: Comparing the quality of human and ChatGPT feedback of students’ writing
papers.finding: 200 human vs 200 ChatGPT feedback pieces on secondary essays: trained humans gave higher-quality feedback in all categories except criteria-based; AI may help for early drafts.

papers.why: Supports teaching students to seek news actively rather than rely on feeds or AI summaries.
papers.title: Social media may hinder learning about science; social media's role in learning about COVID-19
papers.finding: US two-wave panel. Getting news from social media fostered a news-finds-me belief, which left people less informed and more misinformed about COVID-19.

papers.why: Background for misinformation lessons.
papers.title: Who spread COVID-19 (mis)information online? Differential informedness, psychological mechanisms, and intervention strategies
papers.finding: Chinese surveys: misinformed and uninformed people were more likely to spread misinformation; positive-emotion content spread more.

papers.why: Solid pre-GenAI evidence for automated writing feedback.
papers.title: Automated feedback and writing: a multi-level meta-analysis of effects on students' performance
papers.finding: Meta-analysis of 20 studies (N=2,828): automated writing feedback had a medium effect (g=0.55) on writing performance, with high heterogeneity.

papers.why: Background for misinformation lessons.
papers.title: What message features influence the intention to share misinformation about COVID-19 on social media? The role of efficacy and novelty
papers.finding: Korean experiment (N=1,012) on how novelty and efficacy of misinformation affect sharing through emotion and credibility.

papers.why: Strategy feedback matters more than surface fixes.
papers.title: Automated writing evaluation: Does spelling and grammar feedback support high-quality writing and revision?
papers.finding: 119 high school students: strategy feedback plus revision improved essays; spelling and grammar checkers added small gains on some subscales.

papers.why: Tells buyers to ask what a tool adapts feedback to and why.
papers.title: Personalized feedback in digital learning environments: Classification framework and literature review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Review of 39 studies on personalized feedback in K-12 and higher ed. Feedback is mostly adapted only to current knowledge and behavior; few studies justify why a message goes to a given student. Most report positive, mixed, or neutral effects.

papers.why: Supports the draft-then-human-edits theme with a creative writing example for middle school.
papers.title: Lower secondary students’ poetry writing with the AI-based Poetry Machine
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.caveat: Log-data study, no control group, one tool.
papers.finding: Seventh graders in Finland wrote poems with an AI Poetry Machine that offered draft poems. Drafts acted as models students edited and experimented with. More edited versions linked to better final poems.

papers.why: Shows how AI simulation can test teaching methods cheaply; supports explicit spelling instruction.
papers.title: A computational investigation of inventive spelling and the “Lesen durch Schreiben” method
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 3
papers.finding: Neural network agents trained with inventive spelling (reading through writing) did worse at writing and reading than agents trained with a primer method, and reproduced children's typical LdS spelling errors.

papers.title: Bringing Assessment-to-Instruction (A2i) Technology to Scale
papers.finding: Scaled literacy technology redesigned for English learners, K to 3: mixed results; English learners in grades 2 and 3 with weaker reading benefited most.

papers.why: Largest-scale K-12 AI reading evidence in the library; shows a teacher-delivered tool can work in low-resource settings without a curriculum rewrite.
papers.title: Improving reading and comprehension in K-12: Evidence from a large-scale AI technology intervention in India
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Authors are affiliated with the vendor (EnglishHelper) though the paper declares no competing interest; percent gains are not standardized effect sizes; English as a second language context.
papers.finding: AI-based multisensory reading platform in 5,000 Indian government schools, 1 million children, 15,000 teachers, 2016-17. Independent agency ran a randomized control-treatment assessment: 20-40% gain in reading and comprehension outcomes, gains across all proficiency levels. Implemented by existing teachers inside existing lessons with no new pedagogy.

papers.why: Simple, explainable diagnostic idea (fast/slow x right/wrong) that any quiz platform can show students.
papers.title: An interactive test dashboard with diagnosis and feedback mechanisms to facilitate learning performance
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Two classes, one unit, not randomized.
papers.finding: Quasi-experiment, 50 Grade 8 physics students in Taiwan. Dashboard used response time plus correctness to tag each concept as skilled, understood but slow, not understood, or guessing. Experimental class beat control on learning, physics self-efficacy, and technology acceptance; learning gains held for high and low prior knowledge.

papers.why: Important nuance: automatic feedback helps students more reliably than it saves teacher time. Set expectations for time savings honestly.
papers.title: Automatic feedback in online learning environments: A systematic literature review
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Mostly higher ed online courses and pre-generative systems.
papers.finding: Review of 63 studies. 65% show automatic feedback improves student performance; 46% found no evidence it eases instructor workload; 83% found no evidence manual feedback beats automatic. Main method compares answers to a model answer.

children.name: One Text, Many Readers
children.blurb: One Text, Many Readers is the practice of using AI tools to rewrite a passage at several reading levels so that a whole class can study the same content while each student reads a version they can handle.

children.name: Fluency and Reading Supports
children.blurb: Fluency and reading supports use speech tools to give students access to text, either by listening to a student read aloud and marking missed or slow words, or by reading content aloud with highlighting, syllable breaks and definitions.

children.name: Vocabulary in Context
children.blurb: Vocabulary in Context means students learn words best by meeting them repeatedly in meaningful settings, not through isolated lists.

children.name: Peer Review Summaries
children.blurb: Peer review summaries use an AI tool to condense the comments students receive on their drafts into a few clear themes, after names are removed.

children.name: Questions, Groups, and the Teacher's First Call
children.blurb: AI can draft comprehension questions at several levels and suggest reading groups from assessment data, but the teacher must review the questions and form their own groups before comparing them with the tool's suggestion.

children.name: Feedback Students Actually Use
children.blurb: Feedback students actually use means tying AI writing feedback to the class rubric and making revision a required part of the assignment, so that students submit a draft, get feedback on specific rubric points, revise, and explain their changes.

children.name: Grammar From the Class's Own Errors
children.blurb: Grammar instruction works best when it targets the errors a class actually makes, rather than following a fixed sequence.

children.name: Coaching Without Writing
children.blurb: Coaching without writing means using AI to ask questions and challenge thinking rather than to produce text a student would submit.

children.name: Books, Mentor Texts, and Current Events
children.blurb: AI can help students find books they want to read, supply mentor texts that model specific writing skills, and support current events and book discussions at different reading levels.

children.name: Creative Writing With AI Parts Marked
children.blurb: Creative writing with AI parts marked means students may use AI to help draft or spark ideas, but they must show which parts came from the tool, for example by highlighting suggested lines or adding a short note.

children.name: Research and Sources
children.blurb: Students must learn to judge sources because AI chatbots can produce confident summaries containing made up quotes, incorrect dates, or citations to articles that do not exist.

children.name: Integrity: Process Over Detection
children.blurb: Integrity: Process Over Detection means schools should judge how a piece of writing was made rather than rely on software that guesses whether AI wrote it.

sections.body: Reading and writing is the part of school life where AI touches students most often, because nearly every tool can summarize a text, rewrite it at a new level, answer questions about it, or produce an essay on request. The book describes this as both one of the most useful and one of the most important areas to get right, since the same tool that helps a struggling reader reach a history text can let a strong writer skip the thinking that would make them stronger. The Finnish Poetry Machine study is the book's central image: seventh graders received a draft poem and were free to change it, and those who made more edited versions tended to end up with better final poems. The promise and the risk sit in the same place, because a machine draft can be a model to push against or a finished product handed in untouched, and the difference is whether the student does the work of reading, judging, and revising.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that AI works when it is used early in drafting, when it handles sentence level issues while the teacher handles higher order ones, and when peer review sits in between. It does not work when a detector score is treated as proof, when a policy simply bans AI, or when feedback is perfected but never taken up, since one large study found that nearly half of students changed not a single character after receiving feedback. The rule the book holds to is that every idea must name the point where a teacher checks the work, and that integrity rests on process evidence such as version history and conferences rather than on detection software, which exposes districts to unfair accusations especially against English learners. One idea in the chapter carries strong evidence and two carry moderate evidence, while most are sensible practices that still need local testing.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from reading into writing and end with integrity, so a teacher can follow the sequence of a single assignment. One Text, Many Readers, Fluency and Reading Supports, and Vocabulary in Context cover access and comprehension, while Questions, Groups, and the Teacher's First Call and Peer Review Summaries show how discussion and peer work are organized before any machine is involved. Feedback Students Actually Use, Grammar From the Class's Own Errors, and Coaching Without Writing are the writing core, and a teacher would go to them for revision cycles, lessons drawn from student work, and help that stops short of writing the essay. Books, Mentor Texts, and Current Events, Creative Writing With AI Parts Marked, and Research and Sources cover matching students to texts, marking which parts of a creative piece came from AI, and building source skills. Integrity: Process Over Detection is where a leader or parent would go for the board question about fairness, the written policy that names process evidence, and the Thirty Day Move of adopting AI use levels and turning on version history.
sections.heading: How these pages fit together
